## Q1. Tidyverse: New Zealand



### Q1A. Vote Counts by Year and Type

Generate a table of total votes across parties for each year and vote type, sorted by vote count.

 
```{r}
library(dplyr)

nzge <- readRDS("data/nzge.rds")

nzge %>%
  select(voting_type, election_year, votes) %>%
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) %>%
  summarise(total_votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total_votes))
```

### Q1B. Candidate Vote Proportions in 2014

Report each party's proportion of Candidate votes in the 2014 election. Present a table sorted by percentage of votes.

```{r}
nzge %>%
  filter(election_year == 2014 & voting_type == "Candidate") %>%
  group_by(party) %>%
  summarise(total_votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(percentage = total_votes / sum(total_votes) * 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(percentage))
```

### Q1C. Winning Parties by Year

Produce a table identifying the party that won the Candidate vote and the party that won the Party vote in each year.
 
```{r}
nzge %>%
  group_by(election_year, voting_type, party) %>%
  summarise(total_votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) %>%
  slice_max(total_votes, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(total_votes))
```

## Q2. Tidyverse: Tennis



### Q2A. Number of Tournaments

How many tournaments took place in 2019?

 
```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

tennis <- read_csv("data/atp_matches_2019.csv")
tennis %>%
  group_by(tourney_id) %>%
  summarise(n_matches = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  summarise(n_tournaments = n())
```
There are 128 tournaments in 2019. 
### Q2B. Players with Multiple Tournament Wins

Did any player win more than one tournament? If so, how many players did so, and how many tournaments did the most winning player(s) win?
 
```{r}
tournament_wins <- tennis %>%
  filter(round == "F") %>%
  group_by(winner_id, winner_name) %>%
  summarise(
    n_tournaments = n_distinct(tourney_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_tournaments > 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_tournaments))
tournament_wins$n_tournaments[1]

length(tournament_wins$winner_id)
```
12 players win more than one tournament, the most winning player(s) won 5.
### Q2C. Aces for Winners and Losers

Is there evidence that winners have more aces than losers? If using a hypothesis test, remain within the tidyverse rather than using base R testing functionality.

# H0: mean difference = 0
# H1: mean difference > 0
 
```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(infer)
ace_data <- tennis %>%
  select(w_ace, l_ace) %>%
  drop_na(w_ace, l_ace) %>%
  mutate(ace_diff = w_ace - l_ace)

 
ace_data %>%
  summarise(
    n_matches = n(),
    mean_winner_aces = mean(w_ace),
    mean_loser_aces = mean(l_ace),
    mean_difference = mean(ace_diff)
  )

ace_data %>%
  t_test(
    response = ace_diff,
    mu = 0,
    alternative = "greater"
  )
```
p value = 1.530201e-34<0.05, reject H0, there's statistical evidence that winners have more aces than losers
### Q2D. Highest Win Rate

Identify the player(s) with the highest win rate among those who played at least five matches.

```{r}
wins <- tennis %>%
  group_by(player_id = winner_id, player_name = winner_name) %>%
  summarise(won_games = n(), .groups = "drop")

losses <- tennis %>%
  group_by(player_id = loser_id) %>%
  summarise(lost_games = n(), .groups = "drop")

wins %>%
  full_join(losses, by = "player_id") %>%
  mutate(
    won_games = replace_na(won_games, 0L),
    lost_games = replace_na(lost_games, 0L),
    all_games_played = won_games + lost_games
  ) %>%
  filter(all_games_played >= 5) %>%
  mutate(win_rate = won_games / all_games_played) %>%
  slice_max(win_rate, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE)
```

The player with highest win rate is Rafael Nadal whose rate is 0.8695652.
## Q3. Visualization

 
 

### Q3A. Major and Minor Spikes

How many major and minor spikes in cases were there?
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
covid <- read_csv("data/us-states.csv")
daily_cases <- covid %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(
    cases_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )  
# Find the spikes within the 5 observed peak periods
ggplot(daily_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_line() +
 
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily COVID-19 Cases Over Time (first look)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily new cases (seven-day average)",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times. Peaks selected within five periods."
  ) +
  theme(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 35, b = 10, l = 10)
)
```


 
We can see that these are 2 main peaks and 3 smaller peaks. Then, we will need to label these peaks.



```{r}
peaks <- daily_cases %>%
  mutate(period = case_when(
    date >= "2020-11-01" & date <= "2021-02-28" ~ 1,
    date >= "2021-07-01" & date <= "2021-10-31" ~ 2,
    date >= "2021-12-01" & date <= "2022-02-28" ~ 3,
    date >= "2022-06-01" & date <= "2022-09-30" ~ 4,
    date >= "2022-12-01" & date <= "2023-02-28" ~ 5
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(period)) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  slice_max(cases_avg, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(label = paste(
    ifelse(period %in% c(1, 3), "Major", "Minor"),
    format(date, "%b %Y"),
    sep = "\n"
  ))

# Plot the peaks

ggplot(daily_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = peaks) +
  geom_text(data = peaks, aes(label = label),vjust = -0.3) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily COVID-19 Cases Over Time",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily new cases (seven-day average)",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times. Peaks selected within five periods."
  ) +
  theme(
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
  plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 35, b = 10, l = 10)
) 
   
```
I found two major spikes, one in Jan 2022, the other in Jan 2021. I also observed 3 relatively prominent minor peaks, with smaller fluctuations occurring earlier in the series. I treated small fluctuations (especially these early stages in 2020) within the same overall rise-and-fall cycle as part of a single peak rather than counting them separately.

### Q3B. Highest and Lowest Rates per Population

For the states with the highest and lowest overall rates per population, what differences appear in their trajectories over time?

```{r}
# Calculate the avg cases_avg_per_100k rate for each state during the whole COVID period
state_rates <- covid %>%
  filter(state %in% state.name) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Select states with the highest and lowest rates
selected_states <- bind_rows(
  state_rates %>%
    slice_max(mean_rate, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(rate_group = "Highest"),
  state_rates %>%
    slice_min(mean_rate, n = 1) %>%
    mutate(rate_group = "Lowest")
)

selected_states

# Plot their trajectories over time
covid %>%
  inner_join(selected_states, by = "state") %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    color = state
  )) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",
    date_labels = "%b %Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "COVID-19 Trends in States with Highest and Lowest Average Rates",
    subtitle = "States selected by their mean daily case rate over available dates",
    y = "Daily cases per 100k people (7d average)",
    color = "State",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times"
  )  
```
The highest is Rhode Island while the lowest is Maryland.
Both states reached their highest peaks in January 2022, at nearly the same time.
1. Rhode Island had noticeably higher peaks in late 2020–early 2021 and January 2022.
2. The highest seven-day average of daily new cases per 100,000 people was approximately 507 in Rhode Island and 222 in Maryland, making Rhode Island’s peak about 2.3 times Maryland’s.
3. Both states saw sharp declines after their January 2022 peaks. Rhode Island also experienced a noticeable resurgence in the following spring.

### Q3C. First Five Substantially Affected States

Identify, to the best of your ability without a formal test, the first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way.
 
```{r}
# First, look at the early stages of COVID
covid %>%
  filter(
    date < as.Date("2020-05-01"),
    state %in% state.name
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    group = state
  )) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Early COVID-19 Trends by State",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000 people (seven-day average)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
We found that the cases increased sharply since mid march. Take 5 as a threshold of experiencing Covid in a substantial way. 
```{r}
first_reached <- covid %>%
  filter(
    state %in% state.name,
    cases_avg_per_100k >= 5
  ) %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarise(
    first_date = min(date),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(first_date)

first_five <- first_reached %>%
  slice_min(first_date, n = 5)

first_five
```
New York, New Jersey, Louisiana, and Massachusetts were the first four states to reach the threshold for being substantially affected by COVID-19, with Connecticut and Michigan tied for fifth.
```{r}
first_points <- covid %>%
  inner_join(
    first_five,
    by = c("state", "date" = "first_date")
  )
covid %>%
  semi_join(first_five, by = "state") %>%
  filter(
    date >= as.Date("2020-03-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2020-04-10")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = date,
    y = cases_avg_per_100k,
    color = state
  )) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray"
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(
    data = first_points,
  ) +
  
  scale_x_date(
    limits = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2020-04-10")),
    date_breaks = "1 week",
    date_labels = "%b %d",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "Early COVID-19 Trends in the First Substantially Affected States",
    subtitle = "6 states shown: Connecticut and Michigan tied for 5th",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000 people\n(7d average)",
    color = "State",
    caption = paste(
      "Dashed line: threshold of 5 daily cases per 100,000 residents.",
      "Points: first dates reaching the threshold.",
      "Source: The New York Times.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )  
  
```
